extracted.intended_audience: students of algebraic geometry (Math 216), advanced undergraduates/graduate students
extracted.subtask_short: checking regularity and smoothness of schemes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for computing and testing Zariski tangent/cotangent spaces, regularity of local rings, the Jacobian criterion, and smoothness over a field (including base-change and Bertini-type results). Includes exercises and examples illustrating these checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski tangent space cut out by f (mod m^2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Zariski tangent space of A/(f) at a maximal ideal m is cut out in the Zariski tangent space of A by f (mod m^2). Quotienting by f and localizing at m commute, hence the dimension of the Zariski tangent space of Spec A/(f) at [m] is either equal to the dimension of the Zariski tangent space of Spec A at [m] or one less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the linear term of f modulo m^2 to see how f imposes a linear condition on the cotangent/tangent space. Interpret statements suitably when dimensions are infinite. This observation underlies geometric slicing arguments and singularity detection (Exercise 12.1.B and surrounding discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathology of linear approximation at singular points
rubrics_metrics.description: Picking off linear terms (as in multivariable calculus) can fail at singular points: linearizations may cut out a higher-dimensional space than the expected tangent (cotangent space can 'jump up').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the curve cut out by x+y+z^2=0 and x+y+x^2+y^4+z^5=0 passes through the origin; linear terms give x+y=0 (a plane), not the expected line. Use this pathology as definition of singular/non-regular points and as warning that naive linear methods may falsely suggest higher-dimensional tangent spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent-space behavior under intersections and unions
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y and Z are closed subschemes of X containing p, then (a) TZ,p is a sub-κ(p)-vector space of TX,p. (b) TY∩Z,p = TY,p ∩ TZ,p (scheme-theoretic intersection). (c) TY∪Z,p contains the span of TY,p and TZ,p (scheme-theoretic union). (d) TY∪Z,p can be strictly larger than the span.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are structural relations to be used when reasoning about how tangent spaces behave under basic scheme-theoretic set operations; Exercise 12.1.C contains the parts and hints (Figure 4.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian computes Zariski cotangent space
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite type k-scheme locally Spec k[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr) and a k-valued point p, the Zariski cotangent space is given by the cokernel of the Jacobian map k^r -> k^n defined by the Jacobian matrix J = (∂fi/∂xj (p)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes precise the idea of 'picking off linear terms' without analytic deltas/epsilons. Compute partial derivatives formally. Hint: reduce to the origin first; translate for general p (Important Exercise 12.1.G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corank of Jacobian independent of presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The corank of the Jacobian matrix at a point p does not depend on the choice of generators of the ideal of relations (choice of presentation) for the finitely-generated k-algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show appending partials/relations that do not change corank and use elementary column/row operations (Exercise 12.1.H). This justifies using any convenient presentation when applying the Jacobian criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent vectors ↔ maps from dual numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural bijection Mork(Spec k[ε]/(ε^2), X) ↔ {point p with residue field k and a tangent vector at p}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret tangent vectors functorially as maps from the first-order infinitesimal thickening Spec k[ε]/(ε^2) (Exercise 12.1.I). Useful viewpoint in deformation theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension bound for tangent space (regularity inequality)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian local ring (A,m,k) we have dim A ≤ dim_k m/m^2 (Theorem 12.2.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a basis of m/m^2, lift to elements of m and use Nakayama's Lemma to generate m; combine with Krull's height theorem to bound dim A. Equality characterizes regular local rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of regular local ring and regular point
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian local ring A is regular if equality holds in dim A = dim_k m/m^2. A locally Noetherian scheme X is regular at p if O_{X,p} is a regular local ring; otherwise p is singular (non-regular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology note: 'regular' preferred here; 'nonsingular' often used in geometry. Use this algebraic equality as the canonical test for regularity (Definition 12.2.3 and discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian criterion for regularity (corank = dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X = Spec k[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr) has pure dimension d, then a k-valued point p ∈ X is regular iff the corank of the Jacobian matrix (∂fi/∂xj (p)) equals d (Exercise 12.2.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a hands-on method for checking singularity at closed k-points using the equations. Use linear algebra on the Jacobian matrix; extendable to separable closed points with more work (Remarks and later exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular locus of a hypersurface: vanishing of gradient
rubrics_metrics.description: For a hypersurface f(x1,...,xn)=0 over an algebraically closed field, the singular closed points are precisely those satisfying f = ∂f/∂x1 = ... = ∂f/∂xn = 0 (Exercise 12.2.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translation: singular points occur where the gradient vanishes. For projective hypersurfaces use the Euler relation (Exercise 12.3.B) to reduce checks when deg f not divisible by char k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of smoothness over a field via Jacobian corank
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite type k-scheme is k-smooth of dimension d if it is of pure dimension d and admits an affine cover Spec k[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr) where the Jacobian matrix has corank d at all points. A scheme smooth over k is smooth of some dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'relative' notion of smoothness refines regularity and behaves well under morphisms. The definition is local and can be checked on an affine cover (Definition 12.2.6 and surrounding discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness preserved by extension of base field
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is finite type over k and ℓ is a field extension, then if X is smooth over k, X×_k ℓ is smooth over ℓ (Exercise 12.2.F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tensoring and behavior of the Jacobian under base change; converse may require extra hypotheses proven later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking Jacobian corank on closed points suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Jacobian matrix for X = Spec k[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr) has corank d at all closed points, then it has corank d at all points (Exercise 12.2.G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The locus where the Jacobian has given corank can be described by vanishing/nonvanishing of determinants; therefore it is enough to verify closed points (useful for practical checks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness-Regularity Comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: (12.2.10) (a) If k is perfect, every regular finite type k-scheme is smooth over k. (b) Every smooth k-scheme is regular (no hypothesis on perfection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) is proved later (Exercise 21.3.D); part (b) will be proved later as well. Use these to relate the two notions when applicable, but note caveats for non-perfect fields (see cautionary examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: regular ≠ smooth in general
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularity does not always imply smoothness over the base field: counterexample X = Spec k[x]/(x^p − u) with k = F_p(u) where the ring is a field (regular) but the Jacobian criterion fails (df/dx = 0), so X is not smooth over k (12.2.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interchange 'regular' and 'smooth' without checking hypotheses about the base field (perfectness, separability). Additional examples are given (curves with similar pathology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings are integral domains
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m,k) is a regular local ring of dimension n, then A is an integral domain (Theorem 12.2.13). Consequence: at a regular point only one irreducible component of X passes through the point (Exercise 12.2.I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction using slicing by nonzerodivisors and the tangent-space dimension argument; use this fact when deducing geometric irreducibility/local irreducible structure at regular points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular embedding criterion (generators mod m^2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m,k) is a regular local ring of dimension n and I ⊂ A cuts out a regular local ring of dimension d, then r = n−d and there exist elements f1,...,fr ∈ I whose images span I/(I + m^2); Spec A/I is a regular embedding in Spec A (Exercise 12.2.K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct generators by lifting a basis of I/(I + m^2) and compare quotients; use Nakayama and dimension arguments to conclude that the quotient by those generators and by I give the same regular local rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity can be checked after separable base-change
rubrics_metrics.description: If p ∈ X is a closed point with residue field k' separable over k of degree d, let π : X_k := X ×_k Spec k. Then X_k is regular at all preimages p1,...,pd of p iff X is regular at p (Exercise 12.2.N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tensor exact sequences with k_k and compare dimensions of tangent spaces after base change; for separable (or Galois) extensions regularity at one preimage often suffices (Remark 12.2.17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent plane/line via Jacobian linearization
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ A^n is cut out by equations f1,...,fr and X is regular of dimension d at a k-valued point a, then the tangent d-plane TpX is given by the r linear equations Σ_j (∂fi/∂xj (a)) (xj − aj) = 0 (section 12.3.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recovers the familiar multivariable-calculus notion of tangent plane/line algebraically. The Jacobian criterion guarantees these r linear equations cut out a d-plane. Exercise 12.3.H shows independence from choice of defining equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler/Jacobian test for projective hypersurfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective hypersurface f = 0 in P^n_k (k algebraically closed), singular closed points correspond to f = ∂f/∂x0 = ... = ∂f/∂xn = 0. If deg f not divisible by char k, it suffices to check the vanishing of the partial derivatives (use Euler relation) (Exercise 12.3.B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Euler formula deg(f)·f = Σ_i x_i ∂f/∂x_i to relate f and its partials; mind characteristic issues when deg f is divisible by char k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bertini's Theorem: general hyperplane sections are smooth
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is algebraically closed and X ⊂ P^n_k is a smooth subvariety, there exists a nonempty open subset U of the dual projective space P^n∨_k such that for any closed point [H] ∈ U (with H not containing any component of X) the scheme H ∩ X is k-smooth (Theorem 12.4.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Bertini to produce hyperplane sections (or hyper-surfaces) that are regular of codimension 1 in X; often used existentially to choose a single smooth H. Variants (e.g., Kleiman-Bertini) exist.
